2000.problem: Retrieval systems degrade on streaming data without ground-truth labels for unseen topics.
2000.approach: Self-supervised continual learning framework with dynamic soft memory and clustering.
2000.contribution: 27.79% improvement in retrieval without labels; adaptive memory captures evolving semantics.
2000.bp: Real-world search engines and information systems face constant data drift—news, products, user interests all shift daily. A retrieval system that looked perfect on June data can fail in July if it cannot automatically adapt. This matters for every product that serves living, changing data: news search, recommendation feeds, customer support systems.
2000.wh: Training a retriever requires labeled query-document pairs (expensive to maintain) and assumes tomorrow's data looks like today's. Stream retrieval breaks this assumption: new topics arrive with zero ground-truth labels. Retraining from scratch is too slow; static models ignore drift entirely.
2000.ap: CREAM watches incoming queries and documents, clustering them into semantic groups and storing prototypical representations in flexible memory. When a new topic arrives, it measures how different that topic is from what it has seen, then updates its stored prototypes and refinement models—all without needing anyone to annotate ground truth. Three techniques work together: fine-grained similarity matching, regularized cluster centers that don't collapse, and smart sampling to keep memory compact.
2000.ww: Self-supervised learning lets the system learn from raw queries and documents by finding structure (similar documents cluster together; similar queries emerge). The stratified memory acts as a sketch of the topic landscape; when adjusting prototypes, regularization keeps them stable so new topics add signal rather than noise. Adaptive clustering means if the trend shifts, the system recognizes and adjusts.
2000.po: In practice: 27.79% higher success rate and 44.5% better recall on unseen topics vs. unsupervised baselines, matching or beating supervised methods that did have labels. Real retrieval systems can now deploy updates without waiting for manual annotation cycles.

2001.problem: Tropical cyclone forecasting on edge devices requires both physical accuracy and tiny model size.
2001.approach: Spline-parameterized Kolmogorov-Arnold networks reduce parameters while capturing nonlinear TC physics.
2001.contribution: 94.8% smaller model, 68.7% faster inference, 32.5% lower prediction error on cyclone winds.
2001.bp: Tropical cyclones kill thousands and cost billions yearly. Early, accurate forecasts—deployed on satellites and coastal warning systems in resource-scarce regions—save lives. Today that requires powerful data centers; distributing that intelligence to the edge means forecasting without waiting for cloud connectivity.
2001.wh: Physics tells us that maximum sustained wind depends on complex nonlinear interactions: sea surface temperature, pressure, latent heat release all interact polynomially, not linearly. Standard neural networks need thousands of parameters to approximate that. Satellites and edge processors have severe memory and compute budgets—a 19MB model cannot fit.
2001.ap: KAN-FIF uses spline-based Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (which express functions as sums of univariate splines composed together) instead of dense matrix multiplications. Splines are efficient: one univariate spline approximates one variable's contribution, reducing redundancy. The framework layers MLPs, CNNs, and KAN modules, letting each learn its role—CNNs extract spatial features from satellite images, KAN layers capture the polynomial nonlinearities among meteorological variables.
2001.ww: Splines are computationally cheaper than dense layers and exactly suited to physics: many physical laws are piecewise polynomial. KAN's compositional structure (univariate functions composed) matches how weather variables interact—wind depends on temperature and pressure, not on arbitrary learned mixtures. This alignment reduces the "search space" the network must explore.
2001.po: Concrete: cyclone models shrink from 19MB to 0.99MB and run in 2.3ms per forecast on edge hardware (vs 7.35ms). Prediction error drops 32.5%. A satellite processor can now forecast cyclone intensity in real time, sending alerts before traditional systems compute anything—critical for fast-moving storms.

2002.problem: Ocean spatiotemporal forecasting must balance nonlinear dynamics with computational cost and continuous-time accuracy.
2002.approach: Map dynamics to linear Koopman space, use Fourier analysis for continuous interpolation, solve via residual networks.
2002.contribution: 5.6% MSE reduction, 76% faster than diffusion methods, maintains physical constraints in latent space.
2002.bp: Oceans regulate climate, weather, and food security. Accurate sea temperature and current forecasts inform hurricane tracking, fisheries management, and climate modeling. Today's forecasts update slowly; a faster, continuous method opens real-time coastal warnings and climate feedback loops.
2002.wh: Ocean dynamics are nonlinear and continuous in time (eddies, shear, stratification evolve smoothly). Data comes at discrete time steps. Diffusion models generate predictions step-by-step, accumulating noise; each step costs compute. Meanwhile, pure data-driven models ignore physics—they learn statistics but may violate conservation laws (energy, mass).
2002.ap: KFTD uses a two-stage pipeline: first, it projects the ocean state into Koopman space, where nonlinear dynamics become linear (a deep learning insight: many systems linearize under the right coordinate change). Then, Fourier analysis interpolates continuously between time steps using those linear dynamics—no diffusion noise, just harmonic reconstruction. A lightweight residual network refines the result. A physics-informed loss (D-PP) enforces PDE constraints: energy and mass conservation.
2002.ww: Koopman linearization means a few matrix multiplications and exponentials replace iterative sampling. Fourier interpolation is exact for band-limited signals and extremely efficient. Enforcing physics constraints (PDEs) prevents the model from predicting impossible states—no negative temperatures, no spontaneous energy creation—which cuts hallucination and boosts generalization.
2002.po: Empirical: MSE drops 5.6% on average (up to 12.7% for sea surface temperature), and it runs 76% faster than MCVD, a diffusion baseline. Forecasts maintain physical plausibility. A coastal forecast center can now run ensemble models in real time instead of hours later.

2003.problem: DNN watermarks are vulnerable to removal: attackers reverse-engineer approximate keys, stripping copyright markers.
2003.approach: Enhance watermark specificity by decoupling watermark response from approximate keys via adversarial training.
2003.contribution: Robust defense against six removal attacks; watermark remains unforgeably specific to original keys.
2003.bp: Open-source ML models are valuable intellectual property: Llama, Mistral, Qwen. Model theft via replication or misuse erodes incentives to share. Watermarks embed a secret trigger—unique query patterns that only the owner recognizes—proving ownership. If watermarks fail, so does model IP protection.
2003.wh: Current watermarks rely on crafted queries that produce specific outputs. The problem: a watermark is a black-box function, and attackers can query it, measure its behavior, then train a substitute network that mimics it without replicating the original model. Once mimicked, the watermark is removed.
2003.ap: SEW measures specificity: how precisely the watermark responds to its true keys vs. approximate/fake keys. High specificity means an attacker's reverse-engineered key produces wrong outputs, even though it's "close." SEW uses adversarial training: the system tries to find approximate keys (like an attacker would), then updates the watermark to reject those approximations—a cat-and-mouse loop.
2003.ww: Specificity blocks the key extraction path: if an attacker must find *exactly* the right key, not approximately right, the search space explodes exponentially. Adversarial training with multiple candidate keys forces robustness at the boundary of the key space, making approximation fundamentally harder.
2003.po: In practice: SEW defends against all six tested removal attacks—fine-tuning, model pruning, distillation, quantization, etc. Watermark stays embedded and verifiable; the model still works normally on real tasks. Open-source maintainers can now distribute models with confidence in IP protection.

2004.problem: Industrial machines fail; predicting *when* failure occurs is hard because sensor patterns evolve over time.
2004.approach: Identify dynamic stages in sensor streams, learn separate predictive models per stage, update online.
2004.contribution: Higher accuracy, discovers evolving failure patterns, linear-time scalable online learning.
2004.bp: Manufacturing plants lose millions when machines fail unexpectedly. Predictive maintenance—forecasting failure arrival time—transforms costly downtime into scheduled service. Sensors track temperature, vibration, pressure in real time; the challenge is that as machines age, failure patterns change.
2004.wh: A machine that shows subtle vibration for weeks might suddenly accelerate (bearing wear), or it might plateau (adjusted imbalance). Static models trained on historical data miss these shifts. Different lifecycle stages (early wear, accelerating damage, imminent failure) need different predictive rules. Online learning must keep pace without retraining the entire history.
2004.ap: TimeCast segments the sensor stream into stages: early (stable), mid (gradual change), late (acceleration). Within each stage, the interdependencies between sensors differ—early wear shows low correlation, critical wear shows high correlation. The system detects stage transitions from these dependencies, trains or updates a separate LSTM for each stage, and switches models as conditions change.
2004.ww: Stage-specific models capture the right temporal dynamics for each regime—what works for stable machines fails for failing machines and vice versa. Detecting stages via sensor correlation is unsupervised and fast. Online updates (only processing new data) scale linearly.
2004.po: In practice: higher accuracy than end-to-end methods, discovered real stage transitions in industrial data, and runs online with linear complexity. Plants can now forecast failure time within a tighter window, scheduling maintenance more efficiently.

2005.problem: LLMs predict common diagnoses well but miss rare, clinically urgent conditions; they overfit to historical EHR data.
2005.approach: Use deep models to prescreen candidates, then guide LLM reasoning with prioritized evidence from structured EHR.
2005.contribution: 20.65% average gain vs. LLM/deep-only baselines; 30.97% improvement on novel diagnoses.
2005.bp: Electronic health records contain decades of patient history—vital signs, labs, medications, notes. Predicting the next diagnosis saves lives: catching infection early, identifying hidden complications. LLMs excel at reasoning over text but can hallucinate common diagnoses. Deep learning excels at patterns but struggles to explain its picks.
2005.wh: LLMs trained on thousands of cases overfit to the most frequent diagnoses (diabetes, hypertension, infection). Rare conditions (endocarditis, sarcoidosis) appear rarely in training but are time-critical in practice. LLMs also cannot easily extract structure (abnormal labs vs. normal, temporal order) from raw notes. Deep models learn the structure but black-box their decisions.
2005.ap: EviCare runs three pipelines in sequence. First, a deep model (trained on structured EHR) ranks candidate diagnoses, filtering noise. Second, it extracts evidence from structured data (labs, vitals, meds, procedures)—abnormal sodium, elevated WBC, new antibiotic—and prioritizes this evidence by its correlation with each candidate diagnosis. Third, for novel diagnoses (absent from history), it constructs relational evidence: "similar patient with these findings received diagnosis X." All this structured evidence is composed into a prompt that tells the LLM *which* facts matter and *why*.
2005.ww: Hybrid reasoning divides labor: deep models handle the structure-extraction burden (parsing dense timelines), LLMs handle semantic reasoning (interpreting evidence). Evidence prioritization narrows the LLM's focus, reducing hallucination. Novel diagnosis reasoning by analogy (relational evidence) teaches the LLM to recognize unseen patterns it has learned from similar cases.
2005.po: Empirical: 20.65% average gain in precision/accuracy vs. baselines. On novel diagnoses—the hardest, most clinically valuable task—30.97% improvement. A clinician using EviCare sees ranked diagnoses with supporting evidence, making diagnosis faster and catching rare conditions.

2006.problem: A/B testing recommenders is expensive and slow; replacing it with simulation could accelerate evaluation.
2006.approach: Build a multimodal LLM agent that simulates users browsing recommendations in a sandbox, replacing live A/B tests.
2006.contribution: Agent outputs correlate with A/B test results; synthetic data improves downstream recommendation models.
2006.bp: Recommender systems run A/B tests to compare algorithms: does algorithm A increase engagement vs. algorithm B? Live testing is gold standard but costs money (real users see worse recommendations), time (weeks to significant results), and carries risk (negative impact). Simulation replaces testing with synthetic data.
2006.wh: Simulating users is hard: recommendations are visual (thumbnail, title, rating); users click based on visual appeal and memory (I liked that actor, or I'm tired of cooking shows). Real users have fatigue, context, preferences that evolve during a session. LLMs understand language but not visual perception; they don't fatigue or remember sequences.
2006.ap: A/B Agent constructs a recommendation sandbox (multi-page, multimodal—text descriptions, visual features). The agent receives screenshots (page state) and decides what to click, based on its profile (preferences learned from initial context), fatigue (it stops clicking after many items), and memory (recall of liked items). It also integrates macroeconomic or user-context signals to adjust its behavior.
2006.ww: Multimodal perception lets the agent see what users see (recommendations, layouts) and reason about appeal. Fatigue and memory models make behavior realistic—users do slow down and repeat likes. Profile and action memory let the system model individual heterogeneity. Simulated interactions can then train the next recommender generation without live risk.
2006.po: In practice: synthetic user interactions correlate with real A/B test results. Data generated by A/B Agent can train new recommenders effectively. Companies can iterate on recommendation algorithms 10x faster, testing changes in simulation before live deployment.

2007.problem: Global wildfire prediction requires multi-scale spatiotemporal modeling; standard architectures miss long-range dynamics.
2007.approach: Hierarchical graph ODE: represent Earth as multi-level graph, learn continuous dynamics per scale level.
2007.contribution: Outperforms state-of-the-art on long-range forecasting; predictions align with observations.
2007.bp: Wildfires are interconnected with climate: jet streams steer weather patterns that carry moisture; surface temperatures set fuel dryness; atmospheric dynamics drive wind. Predicting global fire activity means understanding this coupled system. Early forecasts enable resource pre-positioning and evacuation planning.
2007.wh: Fires span multiple scales: local weather (kilometers, days), regional atmospheric circulation (continental, weeks), global climate modes (planetary, seasons). Standard deep learning captures one scale poorly or requires massive networks to fuse them. Graph networks handle connectivity but not continuous time; sequence models struggle with long-range dependencies and irregular spatiotemporal grids.
2007.ap: HiGO builds a hierarchical graph: low level = weather grid (local dynamics), mid-level = atmospheric blocks (regional patterns), high-level = global modes (climate oscillations like El Niño). Neural ODE modules at each level learn continuous dynamics: how weather evolves, how blocks flow, how climate oscillates. Adaptive message passing between levels fuses information upward (local weather feeds regional patterns) and downward (global trends constrain local weather).
2007.ww: Hierarchy respects physics: small-scale turbulence averages to regional flows, which cluster into planetary patterns. Learning continuous ODEs avoids discretization artifacts—the model predicts smooth trajectories, not jumpy time steps. Message passing between scales is differentiable, so gradients flow from forecasting error all the way through the hierarchy, improving each level's representations.
2007.po: Empirical: beats all baselines on long-term wildfire forecasts (8+ weeks ahead). Predictions are observationally consistent—they don't violate known climate patterns. Fire forecasting systems can now anticipate seasonal and regional fire seasons with enough lead time to mobilize resources.

2008.problem: Enzyme-substrate data is sparse; knowledge graphs of chemical reactions are denser but their complex interactions are hard to model.
2008.approach: Represent reactions as hypergraphs (multi-way relationships), embed via hypergraph transformer + knowledge graph embeddings.
2008.contribution: Predicts unseen enzyme-substrate pairs by capturing compound interactions in reactions.
2008.bp: Enzymes are biological catalysts that convert substrates to products. Knowing which enzyme acts on which substrate enables metabolic engineering: designing cells to produce medicines, biofuels, food ingredients. Databases of enzyme-substrate pairs are incomplete; building them experimentally is slow and expensive.
2008.wh: A chemical reaction is (educt, enzyme, product) or more complex: multiple substrates → multiple products via one enzyme. Traditional pairwise knowledge graphs (head-relation-tail) miss this many-to-many structure. A hypergraph captures it: one hyperedge connects all participants. But hypergraph embeddings are rare and hard to train; linking them to knowledge graph completion (predicting missing edges) is novel.
2008.ap: Hyper-Enz represents reactions as hypergraph nodes (compounds) and hyperedges (which compounds participate in which reaction). A hypergraph transformer learns compound embeddings by attending to other compounds in the same reactions, capturing global context. Simultaneously, it treats the hypergraph as a knowledge graph (compound-reaction triples) and trains a KGE model to predict missing triples, inferring new enzyme-substrate pairs.
2008.ww: Hypergraph attention captures higher-order interactions: if compounds A, B, C all appear in reaction R, their learned embeddings reflect their co-occurrence. KGE models then extrapolate: if enzyme E catalyzes compounds in reactions with similar fingerprints to a new reaction, infer E acts on the new substrate. Combining both signals (transformer embeddings + KGE reasoning) over-constrains the model to learn compact, generalizable representations.
2008.po: In practice: Hyper-Enz predicts enzyme-substrate pairs unseen in training by reasoning over reaction structure. Metabolic engineers can screen predicted interactions experimentally, prioritizing high-confidence candidates and reducing wet-lab costs.

2009.problem: Fault intensity diagnosis must recognize subtle faults; treating all classes equally misses hierarchical dependencies.
2009.approach: Deep hierarchical knowledge loss: tree-structured soft labels + triplet loss with hierarchical margins.
2009.contribution: Superior fault recognition on industrial datasets; hierarchical knowledge improves robustness.
2009.bp: Manufacturing equipment (pumps, compressors, turbines) degrades in stages: micro-scratches, cavitation erosion, bearing wear, catastrophic failure. Detecting the *severity* of damage (diagnosis) is critical: early-stage faults need gentle maintenance; advanced faults need replacement. Misclassifying early as normal or vice versa costs money.
2009.wh: Classes are hierarchical: "cavitation" is a fault; within it, "mild," "moderate," "severe" differ in intensity. Standard classification treats each class independently. If the model misclassifies mild cavitation as severe, it's a near-miss (both are cavitation) but penalties are equal to confusing cavitation with bearing wear. Also, subtle intensity differences demand fine-grained feature learning that standard losses don't enforce.
2009.ap: DHK loss has two parts. Tree loss creates a hierarchy: same-attribute faults (all cavitation subtypes) cluster together; different subtypes spread proportionally to their tree distance. Focal weighting emphasizes hard examples (borderline mild/moderate calls). Triplet loss with hierarchical dynamic margin picks triplets (anchor, positive, negative) such that margin scales with hierarchical distance: mild-moderate (close in tree) need smaller margin than cavitation-bearing (far apart).
2009.ww: Tree-structured penalties guide the model to learn: faults of the same type share core features, and intensity affects *magnitudes* of those features, not their existence. Triplet loss with dynamic margins prevents the model from over-separating nearby classes (collapsing information) while properly distinguishing far classes. Hard-example emphasis (focal weighting) forces the model to learn the subtle boundaries where misclassification is likely.
2009.po: Empirically: superior results on four real industrial datasets (cavitation sensors from SAMSON AG and public benchmarks). The model reliably ranks fault severity, enabling predictive maintenance to order interventions by urgency and cost.

2010.problem: Trading models overfit to historical regimes and fail when macroeconomic conditions shift; they need robustness to market regime change.
2010.approach: Train robust policy via adversarial Bayesian Markov game; generate diverse, realistic market data with macro-conditioned GAN.
2010.contribution: Trading agent maintains performance across regime shifts; learns from synthetic market data.
2010.bp: Algorithmic trading automates buying/selling decisions to maximize returns. Models trained on 2021-2022 data (low rates, growth stocks) fail in 2023 (rate hikes, value flip). Robust trading requires adaptation to macro shocks: Fed policy changes, geopolitical events, sentiment shifts. Without robustness, backtest performance evaporates.
2010.wh: Market data has temporal correlations (prices trend), cross-instrument correlations (related assets move together), and macro-driven correlations (rate hikes hit finance, help energy). GANs generate synthetic data but often miss these dependencies. Even if data is good, training a policy on one regime creates overfitting: the agent exploits quirks of 2021 that don't exist in 2023.
2010.ap: The framework has two components. Generator: a macro-conditioned GAN uses macroeconomic indicators (rates, inflation, sentiment) as control variables, generating synthetic price paths with realistic temporal, cross-asset, and macro correlations. Policy: a trading agent competes in a Bayesian game against an adversary. The adversary perturbs macro indicators to shift regimes (simulating surprise policy changes or shocks). The trading agent learns a robust policy: one that maintains profitability even when the adversary shifts the game.
2010.ww: Macro-conditioning ensures generated data respects real dependencies—if rates rise, certain sectors react predictably. Adversarial training is a min-max optimization: the agent minimizes loss while an adversary maximizes it. This forces the agent to learn strategies that work across regime boundaries, not just within one regime. Bayesian reasoning (quantile belief networks) captures uncertainty about macro conditions, guiding hedging decisions.
2010.po: In practice: the trained agent maintains profitability across historically different markets. Synthetic data generated from the macro-conditioned GAN is realistic and diverse enough to bootstrap learning. Traders can backtest on diverse simulated regimes before risking capital.

2011.problem: LLMs struggle with domain-specific literature tasks: connecting knowledge across papers, understanding jargon, reasoning within context.
2011.approach: Curate domain-specific literature graphs, define literature-centric tasks (node/edge analysis, related-work generation).
2011.contribution: Benchmarking tool enabling development of domain-specific LLMs; flexible graph curation.
2011.bp: Research fields accumulate knowledge in papers. A biologist must read hundreds to understand the state of enzymatic pathway research; a machine learning researcher must track 10,000+ papers yearly. LLMs trained on all text perform poorly at "find papers relevant to this question" or "summarize the consensus on X in this domain" because they lack structured domain knowledge.
2011.wh: General LLMs see papers as raw text, not as nodes in a knowledge network. They miss relationships: "paper A cites B, B contradicts C, C builds on D." They misuse terminology: "network" means neural network in ML but biological network in biology. Benchmarking domain LLMs is hard: no standard suite of literature-specific tasks exists, and curating domain graphs is labor-intensive.
2011.ap: LitBench automates graph curation: given a domain (e.g., enzyme engineering, quantum computing), it fetches papers, extracts metadata (citations, keywords, authors), and builds a literature graph (nodes = papers/concepts, edges = citations/co-authorship/keyword overlap). It then generates tasks at multiple levels: node-level (classify this paper by venue/year), edge-level (predict missing citation), application-level (generate a related-work section for a new paper). Training/eval splits are generated automatically from graph structure.
2011.ww: Graph-based curation is scalable: one workflow handles any domain. Automatic task generation ensures benchmarks are rigorous and diverse. By embedding papers as graph nodes, LLMs can learn domain-specific relationships during training (e.g., "if A cites B and B cites C, then A should probably know C") and leverage that for downstream reasoning.
2011.po: LitBench enables researchers to develop and evaluate domain-specific LLMs across any field: materials science, climate, neuroscience. An LLM fine-tuned on physics papers with LitBench tasks becomes a physics research assistant, accurately citing sources and explaining connections. The tool democratizes domain-LLM development.

2012.problem: Activity recognition for delivery logistics fails when deploying across cities/sensors; domain shift hurts accuracy.
2012.approach: Tokenize sensor streams, learn domain-invariant representations via selective masking and efficient attention.
2012.contribution: 9.97% accuracy gain over baselines, 6.4x fewer operations, deployed across 4 cities on 2.15B real activities.
2012.bp: Last-mile delivery relies on tracking what delivery drivers do: walking, standing still, climbing stairs, picking up packages. Sensor data (accelerometer, gyroscope from phones/watches) captures these. If the system recognizes activities accurately, logistics can optimize routes, detect unsafe behavior, and improve efficiency. But sensors vary: phone brand, placement (pocket vs. hand), carrier type.
2012.wh: Activity patterns shift across sensor types, placements, and people. An accelerometer on a wrist captures different signals than one in a pocket—same activity, different data. Standard models trained on data from wrist sensors fail on pocket sensors (domain shift). Retraining for each sensor type is infeasible for a logistics company operating in dozens of cities.
2012.ap: GenHAR tokenizes the raw sensor stream (frames of 3D acceleration and rotation) into tokens, each representing a time window. A transformer learns relationships between tokens, discovering which patterns matter (e.g., high-frequency vibration suggests running; smooth curves suggest walking). Selective masking masks out 50-90% of tokens during training, forcing the model to infer missing sensor data—a self-supervised trick that generalizes to new sensor types. Efficient attention (linear or quadratic, not cubic) reduces compute.
2012.ww: Tokenization abstracts away sensor minutiae: a token represents "strong vibration in Z-axis for 100ms", generalizing across sensor types and placements. Masking forces the model to learn robust features that survive missing data—if it can predict a masked token from neighbors, it understands the pattern. The transformer learns these patterns in a domain-agnostic way.
2012.po: Empirical: 9.97% accuracy gain vs. state-of-the-art, 6.4x fewer FLOPs (critical for edge devices on delivery worker phones). Deployed in 4 cities, recognized 2.15 billion activities reliably. Logistics company can now use sensor data to optimize delivery routes and driver safety without retraining per city.
